row.note: The commentary calls the Satanic offer a tree of immortality and an imperishable realm; Genesis says the human might eat from the tree of life and live forever, giving the Eden scene its own guarded version of the desired permanence.

The commentary treats Satan's promise of the tree of immortality as counterfeit permanence; in Genesis the serpent directly contradicts the death warning, so the promised escape from death is itself suspect.

The serpent's denial uses the Hebrew root מות for dying, a concrete cognate of the ayah's يَمُوتُ; here the word is a denied consequence of eating, sharpening the contrast with the condemned person who cannot die.

Genesis uses the Hebrew life root in its statement that eating from the tree could make the human live forever; this is a direct cognate to يَحْيَىٰ in the commentary's contrast between life and death.

Pharaoh orders that every daughter be kept alive (תְּחַיּוּן); the Hebrew life verb matches the commentary's cited Arabic gloss of “let live” as “keep them alive,” including the survival sense rather than mere vitality.

Isaiah addresses the dead as rising and waking from dust, whereas the commentary's damned person has neither death's release nor life's benefit; this is a specific prophetic reversal of that suspended fate.

Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake to divergent outcomes, including everlasting life; this supplies the afterlife distinction that the commentary uses to contrast worldly life with the hereafter and its condemned endpoint.

The commentary adds the Paradise water that revives whatever it touches; Ezekiel's temple river heals its waters and makes living creatures live wherever the stream goes, a concrete life-giving-water image.

The commentary closes by citing Abraham's claim that God kills and then gives life; Deuteronomy puts that same power in God's own speech, making life and death dependent on God rather than on a ruler's threat.

The commentary describes people in fire who neither die nor live; Isaiah's closing image has the rebels' corpses exposed to a worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched, a related but carefully different image of unending judgment.

The commentary distinguishes life as benefit and good from mere biological existence; the Talmud reads “the living know they will die” so the righteous are called living even in death and the wicked dead even while alive, turning the life/death terms into moral evaluations.

The Mishnah explicitly says one hour of bliss in the world to come is better than all the life of this world; this is the closest Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that the hereafter is better and more enduring than preferred worldly life.

The commentary rejects both death and beneficial life for the condemned; Wisdom says the righteous seemed dead to observers but are at peace and have hope full of immortality, preserving an important alternative reading of death's appearance.

A tortured brother accepts death while trusting that the King of the universe will raise him to renewed life; the scene concretely shows why the better lasting life can be preferred over survival now.

row.basis: No resurrection to life for the tyrant
row.note: The martyr says that for the persecuting king there will be no resurrection to life; this gives the commentary's contrast between the condemned state and lasting life a specific judgment scene.

Jesus says the one who seeks to save life will lose it, while the one who loses it for his sake will find it; this reverses the commentary's condemned preference for immediate worldly life over the life that lasts.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; the commentary likewise condemns preferring the near worldly life over the better, enduring hereafter.
The rich fool plans many years of ease from his stored goods, but his life is demanded that night; this concretely exposes the false permanence behind investment in worldly life.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin; this is a specific counter-choice to the commentary's charge that people prefer the near life.
Hebrews explains Moses' choice by his regard for a greater future reward; the commentary likewise ranks the hereafter above the present life and calls it more enduring.
Jesus says the believer who dies will live; this is a direct reversal of the commentary's “neither dies nor lives,” though it concerns the faithful and resurrection rather than punishment.
Jesus adds that whoever lives and believes will never die; this supplies an affirmative, promised form of permanence in contrast to the commentary's barren non-life.
Paul sets sin's wage, death, against God's gift of eternal life; the opposed outcomes make explicit the moral choice between death and lasting life that frames the commentary's contrast.

Paul's resurrection scene says the mortal must put on immortality and death is swallowed up in victory; it gives the hereafter's enduring life a concrete bodily endpoint unlike the fire's suspended condition.
John says the world and its desire are passing, while the one who does God's will remains forever; this closely specifies the commentary's near worldly life versus the more enduring hereafter.

row.basis: Death abolished in the renewed world
row.note: Revelation promises that death will be no more, alongside the end of mourning and pain; unlike the commentary's fire where neither death nor life brings relief, this is death's removal within restored life.

row.basis: River of the water of life
row.note: The commentary cites a Paradise water that revives what it touches; Revelation's river of the water of life flows from God's throne through the holy city, giving a precise Christian paradise-water counterpart.
Jesus describes water becoming a spring that wells up to eternal life; this connects the commentary's life-giving Paradise water with an image of water whose effect is enduring life.

row.basis: Living and dead as distinct states
row.note: Qohelet contrasts the living, who know they will die, with the dead, who know nothing; against that clean division, the commentary stresses the disturbing condition that is neither death nor beneficial life.

row.basis: מות and חיה in one reversal
row.note: Isaiah uses cognates for “your dead” and “will live” in a single resurrection claim; the same death/life vocabulary in the ayah is here joined affirmatively rather than negated.

The Mishnah pictures this world as a vestibule from which one prepares to enter the world to come; this interprets present life as provisional, clarifying why the commentary calls the hereafter the better lasting choice.

row.basis: God leads to Hades and raises
row.note: Wisdom says God has power over life and death, leads down to Hades and brings up again; this expands the commentary's final claim that God both causes death and gives life.

At resurrection the righteous are changed into splendor and live in an enduring order while the wicked wither; this gives apocalyptic detail to the commentary's contrast between the hereafter and the fate of those who reject it.

Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac even from the dead; this is a Christian interpretation of the Abraham story that makes concrete the commentary's closing claim that God kills and then gives life.

row.basis: Departing to be with Christ is better
row.note: Paul says departure to be with Christ is far better than remaining alive; this states a specific preference for the life beyond the present one, matching the commentary's ranking of hereafter over worldly life.

Mark places Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire in Jesus' warning about Gehenna; the Christian reuse shifts Isaiah's corpse image into a warning about final judgment, while still not saying the condemned themselves are alive.

After warning against trust in uncertain riches, Paul urges the rich to lay hold of “the life that is truly life”; this gives a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's distinction between mere worldly life and life as real benefit.
Paul says Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light; this offers a Christian counter-image to the condemned person's unrelieved suspension between death and life.

The Paradise river's tree bears leaves for healing the nations; beside the commentary's water that revives anything it touches, Revelation depicts life-giving restoration extending through the whole blessed scene.

row.basis: Paradise trees and no taste of death
row.note: The saying describes unchanging trees in Paradise and promises that those who know them will not taste death; this is a concrete apocryphal image of the immortality sought in the commentary's false tree offer, recast as a blessed promise.

Moses urges Israel to choose life so that they and their offspring may live; the Hebrew life cognate matches the ayah's life vocabulary, though its immediate setting is covenantal survival in the land rather than the commentary's hereafter.

Revelation calls those who die in the Lord blessed and says they rest from their labors; this complicates the commentary's negated death/life condition by presenting death as a blessed rest for a different group.

row.basis: Death warning before the serpent's claim
row.note: The commentary recalls Satan's offer of a tree of immortality; God first warns that eating brings death, the particular claim the serpent then denies, making this neighboring verse necessary to read the promise as counterfeit.

row.basis: The way to the life tree barred
row.note: After the promise of living forever, Genesis stations guardians at the way to the tree of life; this adds the scene's denial of humanly seized permanence beside the commentary's false offer of an imperishable kingdom.

Isaiah promises that God will swallow death forever and wipe away tears; this is an affirmative restoration in which death ends and life remains, a sharp contrast to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life brings relief.

The psalm asks whether anyone can be ransomed so as to live forever without seeing the pit; against the commentary's counterfeit promise of an imperishable kingdom, it says wealth cannot secure permanence against death.

Ezekiel's temple river nourishes trees whose leaves heal; alongside the commentary's Paradise water that revives whatever it touches, this supplies the complementary healing effect of the life-giving waterscape.
Jesus warns that moth, rust, and thieves undo treasure stored on earth; this gives concrete form to the commentary's near worldly life as a poor choice beside what endures.
Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven where it is not destroyed or stolen; the contrast makes explicit the commentary's preference for the better, more enduring hereafter.
Jesus' judgment scene ends with two enduring outcomes, punishment and life; this closely joins the commentary's fire-bound non-life to its claim that the hereafter is lasting and better.
Jesus contrasts entering life with being thrown into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; this connects the commentary's fire and negated life to an explicit choice between life and punishment.

Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in his lifetime while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and the rich man suffers; this is a specific reversal of preferring present worldly ease over the afterlife.

Paul quotes the death-and-Sheol taunt associated with Hosea to celebrate resurrection's victory; this Christian reading turns the Hebrew prophet's ambiguous challenge into an assured defeat of death, unlike the commentary's unrelieved punishment.

row.basis: Tree of life in God's Paradise
row.note: The victor is promised fruit from the tree of life in God's Paradise; this is the positive, divinely granted counterpart to the commentary's Satanic offer of a tree of immortality.

row.basis: No rest in the judgment fire
row.note: The worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night under smoke of torment; this gives a specific Christian judgment image comparable to the commentary's fire without death's release, while the verse itself does not say they neither live nor die.

Hezekiah says the living, unlike those descended to the pit, give thanks to God; this concretely illustrates the commentary's gloss of life as benefit and good, though its setting is recovery from illness rather than final judgment.

Hosea voices Death and Sheol as powers from which Israel may be ransomed, echoing the commentary's claim that God alone gives life after death; the Hebrew can be read as a threat as well as a promise, so the connection should retain that uncertainty.

Jesus says the believer has passed from death into life and will not come into judgment; this is distinct from the future resurrection promise in John 11, presenting life as a present changed status rather than the commentary's condemned suspension.

row.basis: Visible things pass, unseen things are eternal
row.note: Paul contrasts visible, temporary things with unseen, eternal things; this makes a concrete temporal-versus-enduring contrast for the commentary's worldly life and better hereafter.
Hebrews says believers have no lasting city here and seek the city to come; this gives a concrete formulation of present life as provisional beside the commentary's more enduring hereafter.
Peter describes an inheritance in heaven that cannot perish, spoil, or fade; this specifies what enduring future good means beside the commentary's contrast with the near world.

James compares human life to a mist that appears briefly and vanishes; this makes the present life transitory beside the commentary's enduring hereafter, though it does not itself describe resurrection.
